entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
This course includes the following topic(s): Canadian History: Grades 7-8, Ancient History: Grades 7-9

About World History: Grades 7-9
Read about U.S. and world history from 800-1650AD and ancient history from 3500-550BC through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries as appropriate for student level., Read about Canadian and world history from 800-1650AD and ancient history from 3500-550BC through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries as appropriate for student level., Read about U.S. and world history from 800-1650AD and ancient history from 3500-550BC through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries.

About Ancient History: Grades 7-9
Read about ancient history from 100 BC-350 AD through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. Students will view images, reference maps, and update their Book of Centuries as part of the lessons.

About Canadian History: Grades 7-8
Read about Canadian history from 1800-1900 through books that immerse students in the time period and allow them to see the world through the eyes of those who lived it. Through engaging narratives, biographies, history spines, primary source documents, oral histories, historical fiction, and books that show different perspectives, students come to see history as more than dates and events and develop relationships with people from the past. Viewing images, looking at maps, and working on one's Book of Centuries are also part of developing this relationship.

blocks.text:
• Read through the lesson and gather any necessary links. 

• If you have not read the book, you may want to read the selected pages in advance. 

• Decide which lessons/books to read together and which to have students read independently.

• Connect back to the previous lesson. Have students give a summary of what they remember. (Full narration is not necessary.)

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, teachers may ask a leading question: "What can you tell me about..." Or students may try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Use a picture, map, or engaging question to pique the student's interest in the day's lesson (often included in lesson plans). 

• If necessary, talk about a few unfamiliar words that will be crucial to understanding.

• Read the day's passage out loud or have the student read independently. Sometimes reading for the specified time is a better guide.

• If a book is challenging, try stopping to narrate every now and then rather than waiting until the end. It can also help to read aloud. Or you might want to use an audiobook version of the text and have students read along with it.

• Have students keep an eye out for events or characters to add to their Citizenship Notebook, Book of Centuries, or Copywork Book.

• Have students retell the passage orally or write a narration. 

• Alternatively, students might analyze a character, trace cause to consequence, outline a passage, or use one of the other methods indicated by Charlotte Mason in School Education Chapter 16, especially p.180.

• Students who enjoy writing can experiment with different types of written narrations, but this is not required.

• Give the student an opportunity to share thoughts on the lesson and any connections made (orally or in writing). 

• You could ask them what they thought about the passage or ask an open-ended question to stimulate discussion. Discussion questions are often included in the lesson plans.
• Optional: Add something to the Book of Centuries, Century Chart, Citizenship Notebook, or Commonplace book. If students would like to include pictures, these may be drawn or printed.

lessons.title: 30m Canadian History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Introduction - The War of 1812
⍞ Materials: Jeremy's War 1812

➜ INTRO
Throughout much of the eighteenth century and into the second decade of the nineteenth, the British Navy was engaged in near-continuous naval conflicts until peace was declared in 1815 after the Battle of Waterloo. One of Britain's last major battles before then was the War of 1812, in which Canada, then still a collection of British colonies, became the battleground for a conflict between the United States and Britain over many long-standing grievances, including shipping rights and American expansionist plans. 
The first historical novel we will read in this course is Jeremy's War 1812, a gripping account of the war told from the perspective of a fifteen-year-old orphaned boy who joins a regiment of British soldiers and eventually becomes the personal servant of Sir Isaac Brock. Historical details blend smoothly with a fictional story to create a detailed recreation of this definitive period in Canada's pre-Confederation history.

➜ VIEW
The following video gives some background on the stakes for Canada in the War of 1812 and its importance for Canada's history.
∞ Video Link: The War of 1812 | The Canadian Perspective 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.7-18 "They were expecting me" - "and walked inside."
• Who are the characters you meet as the novel opens? How are they related to each other? What are they like? You may choose to keep a character list with some notes.

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 7-9 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Meeting Sulla
⍞ Materials: A Short History of Ancient Rome, Historical Atlas of the World

➜ INTRO
This year, you are learning about ancient Rome. We are not starting at the beginning with the legend of Romulus and Remus in 753 B.C. We are jumping ahead to 88 BC. The Roman Republic has become a world power. It has marched through the Greek world, razed cities like Carthage, and unseated powerful people. As Pascal Hughes says, "the march of Rome appears unstoppable." 
However, what had once been a republic, which enabled certain people to vote in their leadership, was quickly becoming more of a dictatorship, which is where one person assumes absolute power. There were a number of factors that led to Sulla becoming the first dictator in the Roman Republic. He assumed power through political violence, manipulation of land and resources, and military coups. In 88 BC, the Republic found itself in danger. 
Sulla's story doesn't start at the beginning of his dictatorship. As you read through Sulla's story, make sure to note any questions that come up from the reading. You can either discuss these questions with someone or write them down.

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Ch.6 p.89-99 - end at "political violence tamed" 

➜ LOCATE
⍞ Map Resource: Historical Atlas of the World, p.14-15. Find Carthage, Rome, and any other cities that pop up in your reading to familiarize yourself with the world of Ancient Rome.
lessons.teacherNotes:
• STUDENT TIP
Be sure to add some people, events, and drawings of artifacts to your book of centuries. Mark potential items with a Post-it note as you read so you remember to find something when you sit down to work in your book.

• IMPORTANT DATES

Tiberius Gracchus is elected in 133 BC
Sulla becomes dictator in 82 BC
Sulla resigns as dictator in 80 BC and dies in 78 BC

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 7-9 - Lesson 3
lessons.body:
Spartacus and a Revolt
⍞ Materials: A Short History of Ancient Rome, Historical Atlas of the World

➜ INTRO
Rome was built on slavery. In 73 BC, there were more than a million people enslaved in Rome's Italian lands. As Pascal Hughes says, "Some have been bought from foreign merchants, others taken by military conquest, or enslaved as a punishment for criminality. Then there are the unfortunates who were born into bondage, or who are the victims of kidnap by slavers, or who could see no other option in life than to sell themselves into servitude."
However, revolution came to Rome, and it was led by a slave named Spartacus. There are modern-day movies that praise the bravery of this man and those who rose up with him against the powers that shackled them. Spartacus' story is fraught with bravery and peril, yet it left him a legend in the history books. As you read through Spartacus' story, what sticks out to you? Make sure to note any questions that come up from the reading. You can either discuss these questions with someone or write them down.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Ch.7 p.110-118 - stop at "Third Servile War" 

• How did Spartacus' actions influence the Roman Empire? 

➜ LOCATE
⍞ Map Resource: Historical Atlas of the World, p.14-15. Locate the various places mentioned in your readings.

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 7-9 - Lesson 5

Introducing Caesar
⍞ Materials: A Short History of Ancient Rome, Historical Atlas of the World

➜ INTRO
Around the end of the 15th century, William Shakespeare wrote a tragedy titled Julius Caesar. The story of Julius Caesar captured audiences' attention then, and it remains prominent in our modern-day culture. The blood, betrayal, and scandal of the story is what has led to this story's permanence. But as you will read, there is more to this story. Julius Caesar becomes a famous leader for a number of reasons. As you read through the story retold by Pascal Hughes, consider the many reasons Julius Caesar's story might attract so much attention.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Ch.8 p.128-137 - stop at "even bigger one"

• Why is Julius Caesar's story so infamous? 

➜ LOCATE

lessons.body:
The Métis & The Red River Settlement
⍞ Materials: The Story of Canada; map or atlas of Canada that includes Manitoba

➜ INTRO
While the War of 1812 was at its height in Upper and Lower Canada to the east, a Scottish nobleman named Thomas Douglas, 5th Earl of Selkirk, was working to establish a colony on the prairies to the west, at the intersection of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers, near what is now Winnipeg. Selkirk had received a large grant of land from the Hudson Bay Company and wanted to create a farming community to support many poor Scottish highlanders and Irish peasants, who had lost their homes and livelihoods due to various upheavals at the end of the eighteenth century. This community, known as the Red River Settlement, would come to play a large role in the history of immigrants to the prairies, the Métis peoples, the province of Manitoba, and the history of Canada as a nation.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.114-120 "In April 1806" - "cries of despair."

➜ MAPPING ACTIVITY

∞ Map Link: Map showing the Selkirk Land Grant in 1811

➜ VIEW

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 7-9 - Lesson 25
lessons.body:
The Christian Revolution
⍞ Materials: The Witness of Early Christian Women: Mothers of the Church

➜ INTRO
How revolutionary was Christianity in the Roman Empire? Jesus' teachings challenged a lot of different ideas that had come to be accepted as truths, such as the belief that women were inferior. Mike Aquilina writes, "Males were superior (a man would say) because women were inferior. It was obvious — so obvious that it hardly needed an argument. Fire is hot, water is wet, and women are inferior to men. This unquestioned and unquestionable truth was the basis of all human society."
So what happens when one of Christianity's most prolific writers challenges this idea in his letters? Think about Galatians 3:28, which reads, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." Paul's words would have registered as an attack on Rome's family values.  
Paul promotes the idea that women have a place in society, a place in the Bible, and a place in the early church. As you read through this book, we encourage you to take note of anything that stands out, anything you agree with, and anything you disagree with.

Ancient History: Grades 7-9

· From A Short History of Ancient Rome: What led to the decline of the Roman Empire?

Describe the attitudes and interactions of some of these groups towards each other, as depicted in the novel. OR Write a letter from Sophie to her father, describing all that happened in Beauharnois.

· (The Story of Canada and The Charlottetown Conference): Describe what life was like in Canada in the mid-nineteenth century, in the years leading up to Confederation. OR Explain how responsible government works.

· The Witness of Early Christian Women: Choose a woman in the New Testament and explain how she benefited the church and how she maneuvered through a culture that devalued her.
